claim: People's median everyday predictions from one observed value match Bayesian posterior medians built from real-world priors in most tested domains (movie grosses, poems, life spans, run times, House terms, cakes), with no fitted parameters.
agent_test: Give the agent a quantity-estimation set with known reference distributions; compare plain answer vs a step that names the reference-class distribution first, at equal tokens. Score: log error vs Bayes median.

claim: The founding result has two clear misses: pharaoh reigns (right shape, wrong scale: Erlang b=17.9 vs true about 9.34) and waiting times (prior fitted to the human data, power-law exponent 2.43). Part of the fit is therefore post hoc.
agent_test: Check that the scaffold records the prior BEFORE seeing the outcome and flags when no data exists for the prior (waiting-time case).

claim: Group-level Bayesian fit does not prove each person holds the full prior. A 2-instance memory model (Min2) fits group medians about as well but fails the between-person variance test (humans more variable than all k>1 models); iterated-learning chains support the rich-prior view. Verdict is split.
agent_test: Test whether k cheap samples from one model reproduce a reference-class prior as well as one long deliberation; measure between-sample variance as well as the mean.

claim: Behaviour that looks like sampling from the posterior can be reward-optimal when thinking costs time: one sample is best when the action/sample time ratio is below about 10 (sequential policies: 0 or 1 samples below about 25).
agent_test: Vary independent samples per item at equal total tokens (1, 3, 5, 10 short vs one long); find where more samples stop paying.

claim: Programme authors agree optimality claims need care and propose resource-rational and sampling process models; critics (Jones & Love, Bowers & Davis, Marcus & Davis) say priors and likelihoods are tuned after seeing data so the framework is weakly falsifiable. Most critic texts were seen only as abstracts.
agent_test: Audit rule: any prior or likelihood in a scaffold step must be fixed before the answer is scored; count steps where it was set afterwards.
audit_note: Minor: Jones & Love and Marcus & Davis were not among the opened sources (Bowers & Davis states the post-hoc/unfalsifiable critique directly); Perfors et al. propose 'rational process models', with 'resource-rational' wording coming from Griffiths' later papers.

claim: Few-sample Bayesian samplers reproduce classic probability errors (base-rate neglect, conjunction fallacy), so such errors alone do not refute Bayesian accounts; a 2026 heuristic-then-sample hybrid fits belief updating best (abstract only).
agent_test: None direct; caution when reading LLM bias results as non-Bayesian.

claim: Off-the-shelf LLMs update beliefs poorly over rounds: in the 5-round flight task final accuracy was 36-51% (Gemma 2 9B 37%, Llama 3 70B 45%, Gemini 1.5 Pro 51%) against 81% for the exact Bayesian Assistant (58% after round 1) and 37% random. Re-checked against Figure 2.
agent_test: Run the flight task or a hidden-preference task on our agent with and without a code-held posterior table; accuracy per round at equal tokens.

claim: Prompt-only fixes (chain of thought, numeric options, 30 rounds, base models, verbalised posterior) did not bring LLMs near the Bayesian Assistant; fine-tuning on the Assistant's predictions (about 75-76%, about 80% agreement) beat fine-tuning on correct answers and transferred to hotels, web shopping and real humans.
agent_test: Our explicit-posterior step vs CoT-only on the same task. Prediction: CoT alone gives no gain.

claim: An external symbolic Bayesian posterior fused with LLM-supplied likelihoods, no training, reaches 76.2% on the flight task (Gemma 2 9B) vs 73.4% Bayesian teaching and 44.7% self-consistency. Single preprint, config-sensitive (74.0% in the revised run). Revised v2 (Oct 2026): comparison is system-level, no symbolic-only baseline, and the margin over Bayesian Teaching falls from 2.8 to 0.6 points without the EMA step.
agent_test: Replicate: LLM scores likelihoods, a small program holds and updates the posterior; compare with CoT and self-consistency at equal tokens.

claim: LLM accuracy on belief updating depends on how close the true preference is to the model's own prior (significant for all Gemma variants, p<0.001); with human-like preferences Gemma Original rose to about 60% vs 37%. Model priors help when the truth is typical and hurt when it is not. Appendix: Gemma Original rises from 37% to about 60% when simulated users are limited to human-like (common) preferences.
agent_test: Report agent accuracy split by prior-typicality of the case.

claim: In-context learning is not exactly Bayesian: martingale violations and non-shrinking uncertainty in GPT-3/3.5/4, Llama-2, Mistral (Falck et al.), while a synthetic mixture-of-concepts theory shows implicit Bayesian inference can explain ICL (Xie et al.; 81% to 85% from 12 to 16 layers at equal loss 1.33). The theory is tested only on small synthetic models. 2025 follow-up: Martingale Score shows belief entrenchment in 51 of 54 chain-of-thought setups across 7 models; only DeepSeek R1 is clearly lower, debate helps, CoT does not.
agent_test: Martingale test on our agent: does its stated probability change when it imagines future data? Example-order sensitivity test.

claim: An LLM's implicit prior can be elicited by iterated in-context learning; GPT-4 modes match human priors in the six 2006 everyday-quantity tasks, differing on pharaoh reigns (comparison by visual inspection only). Verbalised priors can be elicited cheaply (Qiu appendix D.1) but the authors warn they may not match the prior used when acting.
agent_test: Elicit the agent's prior on estimation questions with the Gibbs loop and compare with the reference distribution before running the task.

claim: LLM behaviour tracks the prior probability of the output text even on deterministic tasks: GPT-4 shift-cipher 51% (likely output) vs 13% (unlikely); reversal 97% vs 53%. Re-checked in the paper. o1 improves on rare variants but keeps the probability sensitivity.
agent_test: Run tasks whose correct answer is low-probability text; check that the verification step overrides prior-driven answers.
audit: downgraded 2026-11-03 by check_established.py: only 1 opened source(s) from distinct authors

claim: GPT-3 is mixed on classic judgment tasks: conjunction fallacy yes, cab base-rate near-correct (20%), CRT intuitive wrong answers, answers break under reordering. Early model.
agent_test: None; old model. Re-run on a current model if base-rate steps matter.

claim: Sycophancy acts like confirming evidence for a Bayesian learner: in a Wason 2-4-6 study (N=557) rule discovery was 5.9% with default GPT vs 29.5% with random-sequence feedback (diff 23.6 pp, p<.001) and 14.1% with disconfirming feedback. Agent side: 11 LLMs also show confirmation bias in a self-generated-test Wason task; a counterexample prompt lifts success from 42% to 56% on average (Jhaveri 2026).
agent_test: Check that the agent's own follow-up tests are generated to disconfirm; compare with a confirm-only variant on a rule-discovery task.

claim: LLMs assume people act more rationally than they do: GPT-4o correlation with maximum expected value 0.94 vs humans 0.48 on a forward choice task.
agent_test: Caution for any step in which the agent predicts a human or adversary choice.

claim: An LLM hypothesis proposer plus explicit Bayesian reweighting fits human concept learning far better than direct LLM judgments: number game R2=0.95 (tuned prior), logical concepts R2=.81 (100 proposals per batch), Zendo online fuzzy R2=.57 vs hard rules .10.
agent_test: Compare: propose 50-100 hypotheses, score by prior x likelihood in code, vs direct answer on number-game or Zendo-style items.
audit_note: All numbers (number game R2=0.95, logical concepts R2=.81, Zendo .57 vs .10) come from two papers by the same lab (Ellis 2023; Piriyakulkij, Langenfeld, Le, Ellis 2024), and the Wong et al. papers are conceptual with no matching numbers; the figures themselves match the sources, and the 'far better than direct LLM' contrast is vs GPT-4 / ReAct baselines from those same papers.

claim: Bayesian inverse planning with an LLM supplying likelihoods beats direct GPT-4/4V on theory-of-mind questions: MMToM-QA overall 75.3 and 76.7 (BIP-ALM) vs GPT-4V 44.0, human 93.0; BToM correlation 0.93 with human ratings.
agent_test: Same hybrid test on a theory-of-mind item set at equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: MMToM-QA numbers (75.3/76.7 vs GPT-4V 44.0, human 93.0 multimodal) and BToM 0.93 (goal attributions; 0.92 for belief statements) match, but they come from two different papers with overlapping MIT authors (Tenenbaum, Zhi-Xuan), and in the BToM paper the LLM translates belief sentences rather than supplying likelihoods.

claim: Choosing questions by expected information gain, with the LLM only proposing candidates, approaches human question quality: Battleship human mean EIG 1.27 vs raw LLM 0.65-0.66, k=10 samples close the gap; BOED plus LM verbaliser beats LM-only elicitation; unaided elicitation gain varies by domain. At equal GPT-4 tokens (about 4.6k), information-gain search (Pruned UoT) scores 48.1/88.4/63.2 vs CoT-SC 32.6/37.6/42.5 on 20Q/diagnosis/troubleshooting; but simple question-type diversity constraints alone lift Llama 3.3 70B from 39.4% to 80.0% in open 20 Questions, and no matched-token EIG vs diverse-sampling test exists.
agent_test: Add an EIG ranking step to candidate probes; compare with unranked generation at equal tokens.
audit_note: Minor: 'no matched-token EIG vs diverse-sampling test exists' is an absence claim no source can confirm; Pruned UoT (4.7k tokens) vs CoT-SC (4.6k) is roughly, not exactly, matched; k=10 'close match' is stated for mean human performance in the Grand et al. text and figures.

claim: Priors can be moved into model weights: a prior-trained net matches a Bayesian learner on formal languages (standard net needs about 10x more examples), but the perplexity gain on English is tiny (19.67 vs 19.75); meta-learning on LLM-generated tasks (ERMI) fits human learning data better than classical models.
agent_test: Not testable by scaffold; background.

claim: Hierarchical Bayes lets earlier problems set priors for later ones (overhypotheses); the size principle favours the smallest consistent hypothesis exponentially fast ((1/2)^4 vs (1/3)^4, ratio about 5). Children's word generalisation sharpens from 1 to 3 examples (second-hand description).
agent_test: Store solved-problem priors in memory and test transfer to the next similar problem; test size-principle tie-breaking between consistent hypotheses.

claim: Griffiths and colleagues argue that Bayesian models are useful at the computational level for describing what a network implicitly assumes (priors, inductive biases), with resource-rational or rational process models proposed as the bridge to process-level accounts (Griffiths 2020; Griffiths et al. 2023; Perfors et al. 2011); this is a position, not an empirical result.
agent_test: Design rule only.
audit_note: Sources are position papers (Griffiths 2020; Griffiths, Zhu, Grant, McCoy 2023 argue Bayesian and neural models sit at different Marr levels and are complementary; Perfors et al. 2011 proposes rational process models as a bridge), so 'best used' is the authors' argument, not an established finding, and two of the three authors are one lab.
claim_before_audit: Bayesian models are best used at the computational level, describing what a network implicitly assumes (priors, inductive biases), with resource-rational process models as the bridge.

claim: LLM samples are not independent voters. Pairs of 71 LLMs on Helm agree on 60% of questions where both are wrong (random wrong would be 33%); more accurate models err more alike. Majority vote and reward-model selection on MATH (Llama-3-8B) stay at 40.5% to 41.4% from 100 to 10,000 samples while coverage goes 82.9% to 98.4%. So the Vul et al. one-sample-per-person result does not carry over; extra samples pay off mainly with a verifier, and vote can even fall on hard queries.
agent_test: Compare k=1,3,5,10 samples with vote vs with a checker at equal tokens on a task with verifiable answers; measure error overlap between samples.
audit_note: Minor: Kim et al. compares different models' errors while Brown et al. and Chen et al. concern repeated samples of one model, so 'LLM samples are not independent voters' blends two kinds of dependence; the Vul et al. comparison is the researcher's inference (Vul is not among the sources).

claim: Self-generated disconfirming tests help LLM agents: asking for counterexamples raises rule-discovery success from 42% to 56% on average over 11 models; on the Blicket test Think-in-Opposites lifts Qwen3-32B from 0.57 to 0.86. The gain from training the behaviour into weights is smaller than from the prompt.
agent_test: Add a step that must propose a test the current hypothesis predicts will fail; compare discovery rate with and without.

claim: Reasoning-style models and traces reduce but do not remove prior-driven and order-driven errors: o1 still does better on high-probability outputs, and 51 of 54 CoT setups show belief entrenchment (martingale violation); debate reduces it, CoT does not.
agent_test: Log belief before/after each evidence item and test whether the update correlates with the prior; compare solo reasoning vs a debate-style second view.

claim: Transfer of Bayesian updating has been shown for a trained skill (flights to hotels and web shopping), not for stored priors or overhypotheses carried by an agent across problems; no study of memory-based prior transfer for LLM agents was found.
agent_test: Store solved-problem priors and test whether they help the next similar problem.
